identity.title: Redesigning photoprotection: nature-inspired and synthetic biology strategies to enhance crop productivity.

content.abstract: Photosynthesis captures solar energy and carbon dioxide to fuel life on Earth by providing food and oxygen. When light intensity exceeds photosynthetic capacity, resulting in the saturation of the electron transport chain, photosynthetic organisms protect themselves by activating photoprotective non-photochemical quenching (NPQ), which dissipates excess energy as heat. Despite the importance of NPQ in plant physiology, its slow activation and relaxation may cause substantial yield losses in field-grown crops. For this reason, qE, the fastest component of NPQ, has become a central biotechnological target for crop engineering. While pioneering approaches, such as the "VPZ strategy" involving the overexpression of both xanthophyll cycle and PSBS proteins, have successfully enhanced field productivity, their efficacy varies across species, highlighting current biotechnological bottlenecks. This review discusses the molecular bases and activation models of qE in different clades, describing the transition from LHCSR- to PSBS-dependent strategies and the central role of the xanthophyll cycle, while highlighting open debates and unresolved questions. Further, it outlines the future of NPQ engineering, exploring nature-inspired solutions, including the heterologous expression of LHCSR or alternative xanthophyll cycles in crops. Finally, this review discusses how CRISPR-Cas9-driven precision breeding and the application of Artificial Intelligence, and de novo protein design will guide future biotechnological intervention toward developing high-yielding, better resource-efficient crops.
